t: Minimum Subsequence in Non-Increasing Order — Greedy with Sorting
o: We must pick a subsequence whose sum is strictly greater than the sum of everything left behind, using as few elements as possible (and among ties, the largest total sum). To minimize size, each picked element should be as large as possible — so greedily take elements from largest to smallest until our running sum exceeds half of the total. In Example 1, total = 34; taking 10 then 9 gives 19 > 17, so [10,9] works. In Example 2, total = 28; taking 7 and 7 gives 14 which is not strictly greater than 14, so we also take 6, yielding [7,7,6]. With n ≤ 500 and values ≤ 100, even an O(n log n) sort is trivially fast; no fancy data structures are needed.
k: Greedy: taking the largest remaining elements first minimizes the number needed to exceed half the total sum.
Stop as soon as the picked sum strictly exceeds total - picked sum, i.e., picked_sum > total / 2.
Sorting descending automatically produces the required non-increasing output order.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort Descending + Greedy Prefix Sum
a.i: Sort nums in non-increasing order and accumulate a prefix sum. The first prefix that exceeds half of the total sum marks how many top elements to take. This greedy is optimal because replacing any chosen element with a larger unchosen one only helps reach the threshold sooner or with more margin, so the minimal-size answer always consists of some number of largest elements. Ties in size are resolved by taking the maximum-sum set, which the same greedy handles since it keeps adding while the condition fails.
s: Iterate, maintaining cur = sum of taken elements; append each element to the answer.
Stop when cur > total - cur (equivalently 2*cur > total).
Return the collected list (already sorted non-increasingly).
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the single scan afterwards is O(n).
a.sp: O(1) extra beyond the output (or O(n)/O(log n) depending on sort implementation); the result list holds at most n elements.

a.i: Since values are bounded by 100, we can bucket-count occurrences instead of comparison-sorting. Walk counts from 100 down to 1, appending each value as many times as it occurs, tracking the running sum until it exceeds half the total. This removes the log factor and is a nice optimization to mention given the small value range.
s: Compute total and a count array cnt[1..100].
For v from 100 down to 1, repeat cnt[v] times: add v to cur and push v to the answer.
Return the answer (built in non-increasing order by construction).
a.t: O(n + V) where V = 100 is the value range — counting plus one pass over buckets.
a.sp: O(V) for the count array, plus the output.

w: In an interview, lead with the sort-and-greedy approach — it's simple, clearly correct, and generalizes beyond the value-range constraint; mention counting sort as an O(n + V) refinement enabled by nums[i] ≤ 100. Pitfalls: forgetting the **strict** inequality (use cur*2 > total, not ≥), and returning the answer in ascending order after sorting ascending — either sort descending or iterate/collect appropriately. Edge cases: a single-element array returns that element; all-equal arrays may need roughly half the elements. Follow-ups might ask for the solution without sorting (counting sort), or proving the greedy's optimality via an exchange argument.
